Backup File Exposure Checker

Paste your site's URL. This sends a plain GET request to eight well-known backup filenames (backup.zip, backup.tar.gz, backup.sql, backup.sql.gz, db.sql, database.sql, dump.sql, site.zip) and verifies each response against a real archive's magic bytes or a real SQL dump's line shape — not just an HTTP status — before calling anything exposed. It never extracts a matched archive's contents, and it never quotes a SQL dump's row-data statements — only schema statements (table/column structure) are ever shown. See why backup files end up in web roots for the common causes and the fix for each. Only run this against a site you own or are authorised to test.

Run the check

Enter a site URL, then click Check.

Report

Every path checked

PathResult

Prefer a CLI, or hit a CORS wall in the browser?

Most servers don't send permissive CORS headers on arbitrary static paths, so a browser tab often cannot read a cross-origin response at all — you'll see a generic network error with no HTTP status. The CLI has no such restriction and is the one path guaranteed to complete: 

node check.mjs https://example.com/ --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if any path is exposed, so you can gate a deploy on it.

Common questions

Why would a production site have a backup file sitting in its web root?

Usually a one-off manual backup ("let me zip the site before I deploy this change") saved directly into the web-served directory instead of somewhere off the deploy path, or an automated backup cron job that writes its output into the same document root the web server serves as static files. Either way the file sits right next to the site it is a copy of, servable like any other file until something removes it or blocks it.

Does this tool download or read the actual contents of my backup or database dump?

No. Each request reads at most 8KB of the response — enough to confirm a real archive's magic-byte header or a real SQL dump's opening lines, never enough to be "downloading the backup". For an archive, only that header is ever shown as evidence — this tool never lists, extracts, or reads a file from inside it. For a SQL dump, only schema statements (CREATE/DROP/ALTER TABLE — table and column structure) are ever quoted; row-data statements (INSERT, REPLACE, COPY ... FROM stdin) are counted but their text is never shown, because that is where real row content — potentially real customer data — would be.

How is this different from just typing the URL into my browser?

A browser tab shows you the raw response, but many servers return their normal 200 page (a single-page app's fallback route, a themed 404) for literally any path — which can look plausible enough to misread as an exposure, or a real one might download as an unreadable binary blob you can't quickly confirm. This tool verifies the bytes actually match a real archive's magic-byte header or a real SQL dump's line shape before calling anything exposed, and checks eight well-known filenames in one run instead of one at a time. See how this compares to checking by hand.

Is it safe to point this at a URL?

This tool sends only ordinary GET requests to the eight paths under the URL you name — the same requests your own browser already makes when you type one of those URLs in by hand — and it never writes or submits anything. It does not upload the URL or anything it finds to our servers when run in the browser; every request goes straight from your browser to the target. Still, only run this against a site you own or are authorised to test, the same caution you'd apply to any request tool aimed at someone else's server.

Does a clean report mean my deployment has no backups exposed anywhere?

It means the eight paths this run checked either returned a clean 401/403/404 or did not match a known archive or SQL dump shape. It does not check other common exposure paths (a stray .git directory, a .env file, a differently-named backup), does not crawl the rest of the site, and only checks the one base URL you give it. Treat a clean report as evidence about what this run actually found, not a full audit of the deployment.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks eight well-known paths with one GET request each, reading at most 8KB per path. It never writes, submits, or modifies anything, never extracts a matched archive's contents, never quotes a SQL dump's row-data statements (only schema statements), does not check other common exposure paths (a stray .git directory, a .env file, a differently-named backup), and cannot see an exposure at a path it never checked. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the site has no exposure.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every request goes straight from your browser to the URL you name — never through this site, and never logged or stored by us. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day — no site URLs, no file contents, no row data, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

vs-checking-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the Backup File Exposure Checker

Backup File Exposure Checker vs. checking by hand

Typing yoursite.com/backup.zip into a browser tab is a real, fast way to spot the single obvious case: the browser either offers to download a file or shows a 404. It is also the method most developers already reach for first, and it genuinely works for that case.

CheckTyping the URL by handThis tool
Obvious downloadable archive or dumpCatches itCatches it
A server that returns 200 with a generic page for any path (soft-404)Can look plausible enough to misread either wayVerified against a real archive's magic bytes or a real SQL dump's line shape before calling anything exposed
Checking all eight common backup filenames, not just oneManual, easy to stop after trying the one you thought ofChecks backup.zip, backup.tar.gz, backup.sql, backup.sql.gz, db.sql, database.sql, dump.sql, and site.zip every run
Confirming a match without reading row data by handOpening the file to check risks reading real row contentConfirms from the header/structural shape alone; row-data statements are counted, never quoted
Repeatable in CI on every deployManual, point-in-timeCLI returns a real exit code

When to still just look

If you only need a one-off sanity check on a URL you're already typing into the address bar, looking is fine — it's free and you're already there. The gap this tool closes is coverage and confidence: all eight relevant filenames, not just the one you thought to try, each verified against real structural evidence rather than eyeballed, every time a deploy happens, with an exit code a CI pipeline can act on.

Common questions

What does typing the URL into a browser tab actually show you?

Typing yoursite.com/backup.zip into a browser tab is a fast, real check for the single obvious case: the browser either offers to download a file or shows a 404. If it downloads, you don't need a tool to tell you it's exposed -- though you may not notice whether the downloaded file is actually a real archive or just some other binary-looking response until you open it.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Three ways this scripted check catches and a quick manual look easily misses: (1) a server that returns its normal 200 page (a single-page app's fallback route, a themed 404) for literally any path -- a download prompt or a page that loads without obviously erroring can be misread either way without checking the actual bytes. (2) Checking only the one filename you thought to try, not the seven other common ones (backup.tar.gz, backup.sql, backup.sql.gz, db.sql, database.sql, dump.sql, site.zip) a backup script or a careless one-off save could have used. (3) Opening a downloaded file to confirm it's real, and to see what's inside, risks reading actual row data by hand -- this tool confirms a match from the file's header or structural shape alone and deliberately never shows row-data content.

Why does this matter for CI, not just a one-time check?

A manual check is a point-in-time look. A new backup script, a forgotten one-off save, or a server configuration change can reintroduce this exposure at any point after the last time someone happened to check. The CLI here returns a real exit code, so it can gate a deploy the same way a linter or test suite does -- catching a regression the day it ships rather than the next time someone thinks to check by hand.

why-backup-files-end-up-in-web-roots.htm.text:
← Back to the Backup File Exposure Checker

Why backup files end up in web roots

A backup archive or SQL dump only becomes a problem when a production deployment leaves it publicly reachable. There are four common, independent ways that happens, and each has its own fix — fixing one does not fix the others.

1. A backup script writes its output into the served directory

A cron job or deploy hook that runs tar -czf backup.tar.gz . or mysqldump mydb > backup.sql from inside the web root writes its output right next to the site it is a copy of — servable like any other file the moment it lands. 

# Wrong: backup written straight into the served directory
cd /var/www/myapp && tar -czf backup.tar.gz .

# Right: written outside the served tree entirely
mysqldump mydb | gzip > /var/backups/myapp/db-$(date +%F).sql.gz

2. A one-off manual backup gets left where it was made

"Let me zip the site before I deploy this change" is a real, common reason a backup.zip appears — made once, in the web root, purely for convenience, and then forgotten once the deploy went fine. Treat any backup made inside the deploy path as temporary: move it out or delete it the same day.

3. No server rule blocking backup extensions as a second layer

Defense in depth: even with the backup process fixed, a server or CDN rule that denies requests for common backup extensions means a stray copy — a one-off manual backup, a misconfigured mirror — is not actually reachable. 

# nginx example
location ~* \.(zip|tar\.gz|sql|sql\.gz|bak)$ { deny all; return 404; }

# Apache example (.htaccess in the document root)
<FilesMatch "\.(zip|tar\.gz|sql|sql\.gz|bak)$">
  Require all denied
</FilesMatch>

4. Backups are kept as files at all, instead of a managed off-box service

A dedicated backup service or object-storage bucket with its own access controls never puts the file anywhere a web server could serve it in the first place — it is both safer and more reliable than any deploy-path convention.

If this checker already found an exposure

Fix the process cause first (steps 1–2 above), then treat every credential and secret that archive or dump's tables could hold as compromised and rotate it immediately — database passwords, API keys, session secrets, anything a config file or environment table inside the backup could have carried. Rotation is the only remedy once a backup has been served publicly, even once: there is no way to know for certain it was not already fetched by an automated scanner before you found it.

Run the Backup File Exposure Checker against your production URL to see which of these, if any, apply to your deployment right now. Only run it against a site you own or are authorised to test.
